12	### 1. The Founding, the Station, and the Fatal Purchase (1889–1897)
13	
14	In 1889, valley farmers, weary of hauling their butter all the way to Ashlin, met at the Larrow
15	Green schoolhouse and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. They elected
16	Gideon Vose — "a heavy, quiet, obstinate man who had once thought of the law and thought better of
17	it" — as first president; he wrote the Association's by-laws himself, at his own kitchen table.
18	This comes from Dell Rundle's 1939/1959 jubilee pamphlet, "The Larrow Valley Creamery: Fifty
19	Years," the main secondary history of the founding.
20	
21	In 1891 the Association built its creamery at Larrow Green, on the creek below the mill, and paid
22	the valley in cash monthly for the first time. That same year (per Rundle, who quotes the text
23	directly — preferred over a rival 1893 date given only as a vague secondhand "impression" in a
24	1919 letter) the Association adopted Article VII: patrons would be paid by the butterfat test of
25	the station where they delivered, not by the weight of milk. That sentence would later be called
26	"the hinge of the whole matter."
27	
28	On 4 May 1896 (the most precise date, from Orin Falke's 1959 county report, independently matched
29	by "May 1896" in buttermaker Hobart Sill's 1934 retirement remarks), the Association opened a
30	second station at Ostrey Hollow, seven miles up the valley (three independent sources agree on
31	"seven"), serving the Hessel Bottom farms. Ansel Keddie was appointed tester and separator man
32	there — a post he held for 29 unbroken seasons, to 1925. The station opened with no glassware of
33	its own; Sill lent his own testing equipment from Larrow Green for the first season.
34	
35	The station's own outfit arrived 1 May 1897 — the best-supported of four competing dates
36	(1897/1898/1899/1922), corroborated by a supplier's invoice, a company history, and a tester's
37	wife's diary. Ammon & Sons' invoice, dated 14 April 1897, itemizes 6 dozen milk-test pipettes, 12
38	dozen test bottles, an acid measure, and a hand tester, totaling either $77.93 (summing the line
39	items) or $77.39 (the supplier's own prose figure — an unresolved discrepancy within that one
40	source). This unremarkable purchase is the origin of a defect that went undetected for 26 years.
41

46	there than the same herds' milk tested at Larrow Green. Management did not believe them.
47	
48	One such patron, Emmet Brant, began keeping his own private weigh-book — starting either 1 January
49	1900 (per his granddaughter Hazel Brant, speaking in 1981) or 1 January 1897 (per his nephew Duncan

51	the sources.
